title: Strategies of the Freedom Struggle

cards.b:
India's freedom struggle was not one movement with one method. Over 62 years, from the Congress's founding in 1885 to independence in 1947, leaders tried petitions, boycotts, mass satyagraha, council politics, armed revolution and an army in exile. Part of the story is also about how they argued over methods.

This is the main exam angle. UPSC asks you to compare strategies, not to list events. Three questions to carry: Who led and who joined? What was the method? What did it achieve and fail to achieve?

The topic opens Paper I Section B. Good answers link events to the ideology behind them, which connects to the later lessons on peasants, workers and perspectives (liberal, socialist, Marxist, radical humanist, Dalit).

Moderates used petition and prayer; Extremists boycott and swadeshi; Gandhi mass satyagraha. Others entered councils, took up arms, or (the INA) raised an army abroad. The strategies overlapped. A Gandhian movement could run alongside council entry, and revolutionaries worked in parallel. Bipan Chandra's India's Struggle for Independence (1988) describes the Gandhian pattern as Struggle-Truce-Struggle (S-T-S), with a constitutional wing working between phases to keep the movement fresh.

The Indian National Congress was founded in December 1885 in Bombay, with A.O. Hume as organiser and W.C. Bonnerjee as first president.

The Moderates (Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Pherozeshah Mehta, Surendranath Banerjea, Ranade) trusted British fairness. Their method was often called prayer, petition and protest. They demanded:

  • More Indians in councils and services (simultaneous ICS exams in India).
  • Reduction of military spending and land revenue.
  • An end to the "drain of wealth" (Naoroji, Poverty and Un-British Rule in India, 1901; also R.C. Dutt).

Gains: the Indian Councils Act 1892 and economic criticism that undermined the claim of benevolent rule. Limits: a narrow elite base, and little mass contact. Radicals called it "political mendicancy".

Lord Curzon announced the Partition of Bengal in July 1905; it took effect on 16 October 1905. Bengal's response launched the Swadeshi and Boycott Movement.

  • Lal-Bal-Pal (Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal) with Aurobindo pushed for swaraj, which Tilak called a birthright.
  • The four planks: swadeshi, boycott of foreign goods, national education (National Council of Education, 1906) and passive resistance.
  • Tilak used festivals (Ganapati, Shivaji) to mobilise people.
  • The Congress split at Surat in 1907. Repression followed: Tilak was jailed for six years in 1908.

The Muslim League was formed in 1906, and Morley-Minto reforms (1909) introduced separate electorates. Bengal partition was annulled in 1911. The Home Rule Leagues (Tilak and Annie Besant, 1916) and the Lucknow Pact (Dec 1916) revived unity.

Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915. His method, satyagraha (insistence on truth), was based on non-violence, willingness to suffer and an appeal to the opponent's conscience. His first Indian experiments were local:

  • Champaran (1917): indigo cultivators against the tinkathia system.
  • Ahmedabad (1918): mill workers' wage dispute, with a fast.
  • Kheda (1918): peasants and revenue remission after crop failure.

In 1919, against the Rowlatt Act, he called the first all-India hartal. The Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April 1919, Amritsar) turned moderate hopes into anger, and the Khilafat issue gave a chance to join Hindus and Muslims.

New features: mass base (peasants, women, workers), non-violence, a Hindi-speaking style and the Congress as a mass organisation.

• Non-Cooperation (adopted 1920): boycott of courts, schools, councils and foreign cloth, with khadi and national institutions. It was suspended by Gandhi after violence at Chauri Chaura (5 February 1922).
  • Civil Disobedience: after the Lahore session (December 1929) declared Purna Swaraj, 26 January 1930 became Independence Day. The Dandi march (12 March-6 April 1930) broke the salt law. Gandhi-Irwin Pact: 5 March 1931. Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference in 1931. The movement was resumed and withdrawn by 1934.
  • The Communal Award (August 1932) and the Poona Pact (24 September 1932) between Gandhi and Ambedkar settled depressed-class representation.

When mass movements paused, the constitutional path kept political life active.

  • Swaraj Party (January 1923): C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru, who wanted to enter councils and "wreck from within". They used walkouts and defeated government bills. Opposed by the "No-Changers" (Rajagopalachari, Rajendra Prasad).
  • Simon Commission (1927): all-white, boycotted by most. Lajpat Rai died after a police lathi-charge in 1928. The Nehru Report (1928) was the Indian reply, a draft constitution.
  • Government of India Act 1935: provincial autonomy. In the 1937 elections, the Congress won a majority in 5 of 11 provinces and formed ministries in several more. The ministries resigned in 1939 over India's entry into World War II.

Congress leaders Nehru, Bose and the socialists disliked office-taking, but it brought administrative experience and mass contact.

• Early revolutionaries: the Chapekar brothers (Pune, 1897), the Anushilan Samiti in Bengal, and Ghadar Party in North America (1913). Abroad: Shyamji Krishnavarma, Madame Cama, V.D. Savarkar.
  • HRA and HSRA: the Hindustan Republican Association (1924, Ram Prasad Bismil, Sachindranath Sanyal) and the Kakori train action (1925). Later, the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (1928) with Chandrashekhar Azad, Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru. Bhagat Singh, an atheist socialist, threw a bomb in the Central Assembly (April 1929) and was hanged in March 1931. Surya Sen led the Chittagong armoury raid (April 1930).
  • Subhas Chandra Bose left Congress in 1939 (Forward Bloc), reached Germany and then Southeast Asia. He took charge of the Indian National Army in 1943 and set up the Azad Hind government in Singapore. The INA trials (Red Fort, November 1945) stirred public feeling and shook the loyalty of Indian soldiers.

• August Offer (1940) and individual satyagraha (1940-41). The Cripps Mission (March 1942) offered post-war dominion status with an option for provinces to stay out, and was rejected.
  • Quit India: 8 August 1942 (Bombay Gowalia Tank). "Do or Die." Leaders were arrested on 9 August, and the movement became a leaderless mass uprising, with parallel governments in Ballia, Tamluk and Satara. Aruna Asaf Ali, Jayaprakash Narayan and Usha Mehta (Congress radio) became symbols.
  • 1945-47: Wavell's Simla Conference (1945), INA trials, the Royal Indian Navy mutiny (February 1946), the Cabinet Mission (1946), Direct Action Day (16 August 1946), Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947) and the Indian Independence Act (18 July 1947).

Independence came on 15 August 1947 along with Partition.

cards.h: Why did India become free? Historians disagree
cards.b:
• Nationalist view (Bipan Chandra and others, India's Struggle for Independence, 1988): a broad anti-colonial movement under Gandhi's leadership forced the end of British rule.
  • Cambridge School (Anil Seal, John Gallagher, Gordon Johnson): Indian politics was a competition among local elites for state patronage, and nationalism was a cover.
  • Marxist (R.P. Dutt, India Today, 1940; A.R. Desai): the movement was led by the bourgeoisie, who compromised with imperialism to protect class interests.
  • Subaltern Studies (Ranajit Guha, from 1982): elite nationalism ignored peasants and tribals, who had their own autonomous politics.
  • Other factors: World War II weakened Britain, the INA and naval mutiny shook the Raj's loyalty, and the Labour government was ready to leave.

A strong answer weighs several causes, not one.

• Constitution: the Karachi resolution (1931) promised fundamental rights and economic programme. The Nehru Report of 1928 shaped Part III and ideas on minorities. The 1935 Act supplied much of the Constitution's structure.
  • Political style: hartals, padyatras, fasts and civil disobedience are still used. The Anna Hazare movement (2011) and the farmers' protests of 2020-21 echoed Gandhian methods, with debates on whether they matched them.
  • Memory politics: Azadi Ka Amrit Mahotsav (launched in March 2021, concluded in 2023) and debates about forgotten heroes, tribal leaders like Birsa Munda and women freedom fighters.
  • Open questions: is Gandhian non-violence a universal method or a product of its time? Debates about Bose, Bhagat Singh and the role of armed struggle also continue.

"The Gandhian strategy of struggle-truce-struggle was an effective approach to the freedom struggle." Discuss.
Compare the Moderate and Extremist methods.
Assess the role of constitutional struggle in the national movement.
How did revolutionary and INA activities complement mass movements?

Structure: frame the strategies in a table, then give each phase in date order with its leaders, method, gains and limits. For S-T-S, link the mass phases (1920-22, 1930-34, 1942) to the constitutional gaps. Use the historiography debate for analysis. Close by saying that strategies were complementary and that the war and the INA shifted the final timing.
